title: The Town That Vanished from the Map

pages.text: Ayisha and her cousin Kwabla walked along a path near Hani, in the Bono region of Ghana. All around were farms, trees and low grassy mounds. “Nothing here,” said Kwabla. Nana Afriyie, an elder, smiled. “Under your feet,” he said, “stood a busy town called Begho.”
sentences: Ayisha and her cousin Kwabla walked along a path near Hani, in the Bono region of Ghana.
All around were farms, trees and low grassy mounds.
“Nothing here,” said Kwabla.
Nana Afriyie, an elder, smiled.
“Under your feet,” he said, “stood a busy town called Begho.”
pages.alt: Two children and an elder stand on grassy mounds in a quiet farming landscape.

pages.text: “Begho was a trading town,” said Nana Afriyie. “Gold, kola nuts, cloth and brass passed through it. Akan-speaking Bono people lived here, and merchants who came from the north.” “How old is it?” asked Ayisha. “People say it is very old,” said Nana Afriyie. “Sources do not fully agree on when it began. Some give around the eleventh century, but we will see that the evidence is not simple.”

Akan-speaking Bono people lived here, and merchants who came from the north.” “How old is it?” asked Ayisha.

“Sources do not fully agree on when it began.
Some give around the eleventh century, but we will see that the evidence is not simple.”
pages.alt: A bustling market of traders with kola nuts, gold and cloth, drawn as a story picture.

pages.text: Dr Mensima, an archaeologist, was sorting broken pottery at a table. “In the twentieth century, teams from the University of Ghana dug here, and later worked with colleagues from the United States,” she said. “We found at least five quarters, or neighbourhoods, and between a thousand and fifteen hundred house mounds. We estimate that at its busiest, maybe seven to ten thousand people lived in Begho. Those are estimates, not exact counts.”

“In the twentieth century, teams from the University of Ghana dug here, and later worked with colleagues from the United States,” she said.

We estimate that at its busiest, maybe seven to ten thousand people lived in Begho.
Those are estimates, not exact counts.”
pages.alt: An archaeologist shows pottery pieces and a site plan to the children.

pages.text: “How can you tell?” asked Kwabla. “From clues,” said Dr Mensima. “Pottery scattered over a huge area, house floors, tools, brass, and charcoal we can date with radiocarbon tests. Some of those dates are earlier than the date people usually give for the start of the town. So when Begho began is still a question.” Ayisha wrote: clues = pottery, floors, tools, charcoal. Start date: not settled.

pages.text: “So what happened to Begho?” asked Ayisha. Nana Afriyie spoke slowly. “Our oral history says the Asante army destroyed the town and its people scattered. The tellings place this around the middle of the 1700s. People in towns like Bondoukou and Kong trace their families to refugees from Begho.”
sentences: “So what happened to Begho?” asked Ayisha.
Nana Afriyie spoke slowly.
“Our oral history says the Asante army destroyed the town and its people scattered.
The tellings place this around the middle of the 1700s.
People in towns like Bondoukou and Kong trace their families to refugees from Begho.”
pages.alt: An elder speaks while children listen, with a faint picture of people leaving a town.

pages.text: “But the digging tells a more complicated story,” said Dr Mensima. “Some evidence suggests people lived here, in smaller numbers, into the early 1800s. So two accounts give two different times for the end. Perhaps the town was attacked and then slowly emptied. Perhaps the dates are not exact. We do not know yet, and we have excavated only certain parts, so we do not have the full picture.”

pages.alt: A chart compares two timelines: destroyed in the 1700s, and slowly shrinking into the 1800s.

pages.text: “Is one of you wrong?” asked Kwabla. “Not necessarily,” said Dr Mensima. “Oral history and archaeology are different kinds of evidence. Elders remember how the story was carried through families. Archaeologists read what the ground kept. Where they agree, we trust the story more. Where they differ, we ask more questions.”

Where they differ, we ask more questions.”
pages.alt: An elder and an archaeologist stand side by side, looking at the same mound.

pages.text: Before leaving, the children wrote on a card: Begho was real and large. It was a trading town of gold and kola. How it ended: not settled. “Please,” said Nana Afriyie, “do not take pottery or dig here. The ground is a book, and a book torn apart cannot be read.” Ayisha nodded. “We will learn from it, and leave it.” The end.

activities.question: What was Begho known for?
options: Trade in gold, kola, cloth and brass

activities.prompt: The elders say Begho was destroyed in the mid-1700s. The digs suggest people stayed longer. What might explain both?
options: The town may have been attacked and then slowly emptied

activities.question: Why did Dr Mensima say oral history and archaeology are different kinds of evidence?
options: One comes from remembered stories and the other from what the ground kept
One is true and the other is false

activities.definition: A scientist who studies the past by digging up and examining old objects and buildings.

activities.prompt: Put the story of Begho in order.
items: Begho grew as a trading town.
Archaeologists dug at the site in the twentieth century.
Oral history says the town was destroyed and people scattered.
Historians still debate exactly how it ended.

activities.prompt: Nana Afriyie said the ground is like a book. How do you feel about protecting places where history is buried?
